outline_section.section_title: Introduction to Convolution as Overlap Area
outline_section.learning_goal: Explain that, for one fixed output time, convolution produces a number by taking the signed area under the product $x(\tau)h(t-\tau)$ over the part of the $\tau$-axis where the two signals overlap.

image_policy.image_description_seed: A clean convolution-overlap diagram on a shared $\tau$-axis: one simple positive rectangular $x(\tau)$, one flipped-shifted rectangular $h(t-\tau)$ at a fixed t, the overlap interval shaded, and a product-area panel showing the signed area that becomes $y(t)$.
visual_elements: finite-duration $h(t-\tau)$ plot with t marked as fixed
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Use simple rectangular pulses and a single fixed t so the visual reduces load by connecting overlap, product, area, and output value without introducing case analysis.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Teach the overlap-area interpretation of the convolution integral for one fixed output time.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Use two nonnegative rectangular signals with a clear partial overlap so the product area is a single positive rectangle.
paragraph_plan: Recall the convolution formula and state that t is fixed while $\tau$ runs across the input timeline.
Explain that $x(\tau)$ and $h(t-\tau)$ only contribute where both are nonzero on the same $\tau$-interval.
Connect pointwise multiplication to a product signal whose area over $\tau$ becomes one scalar output value.
State that positive products add area, negative products subtract area, and no overlap gives zero area.
Close by framing the lesson as practice reading output values from overlap area rather than performing full piecewise convolution mechanics.

outline_section.handoff_notes: Keep the tutorial compact and visual; do not introduce moving-t case boundaries or full convolution plots.

outline_section.section_title: Interpreting the Product Area for a Fixed Output Time
outline_section.learning_goal: Given plots of $x(\tau)$ and $h(t_0-\tau)$ for one fixed output time, read the overlap interval, form the product height, and interpret the product area as $y(t_0)$.

image_policy.image_description_seed: Two aligned rectangular signal plots on the same $\tau$-axis for a fixed output time t0, with the overlap interval shaded and a small product-area panel below.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Use visually simple intervals and integer heights so the example writer can focus on interpreting the overlap area, not algebraic setup.

question_policy.answer_format: signed numeric value for the fixed output, such as $y(2)=4$
question_policy.practice_question_model: A graph shows $x(\tau)=2$ on $0\le \tau\le 2$ and zero elsewhere, and $h(1-\tau)=1$ on $-1\le \tau\le 1$ and zero elsewhere. Interpret $y(1)$ as overlap area.
distractor_plan: Anticipate using the union length instead of the overlap length.
Anticipate forgetting to multiply the signal heights.
Anticipate reporting only the overlap interval rather than the area.
Anticipate treating t as a variable instead of the fixed output time.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: At fixed output time $t=2$, a graph shows $x(\tau)=1$ on $0\le \tau\le 3$ and $h(2-\tau)=2$ on $1\le \tau\le 4$, with both signals zero elsewhere. Interpret $y(2)$ as an overlap area.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Conclude that the overlap is $1\le \tau\le 3$, the product height is 2, and $y(2)=4$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This is the first active use of the tutorial schema for one fixed output time.
solution_step_plan: State that t is fixed at 2, so the only variable being scanned is $\tau$.
Read the support of $x(\tau)$ from the plot.
Read the support of $h(2-\tau)$ from the plot.
Find the overlap interval of the two supports.
Multiply the heights on the overlap and compute the rectangle area.
State the area as the convolution output value $y(2)$.
practice_variation_axes: Vary the fixed output time label.
Vary rectangular support endpoints while keeping one overlap interval.
Vary simple positive heights.
Keep the product as one rectangle.

outline_section.handoff_notes: The example should establish the fixed-t area-reading routine before adding sign or comparison wrinkles.

prompt_blocks.text: At fixed output time $t=1$, the graph shows $x(\tau)=2$ on $0\le \tau\le 2$ and $h(1-\tau)=1$ on $-1\le \tau\le 1$, with both signals zero elsewhere.
Use the overlap area to find $y(1)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The common nonzero interval is $0\le \tau\le 1$, so the overlap width is 1. On that interval, the product height is $2\cdot 1=2$, giving area $2\cdot 1=2$.

outline_section.section_title: Reading Positive Overlap Area from Two Positive Signals
outline_section.learning_goal: Recognize that when both overlapping signal values are positive, the product area contributes a positive amount to the convolution output.

image_policy.image_description_seed: Aligned plots of two positive finite-duration signals on a $\tau$-axis, with the overlap shaded and the positive product region shown above the axis.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Use nonnegative rectangular signals with visible positive heights; keep all product values above the axis.

question_policy.practice_question_model: A graph shows $x(\tau)=1$ on $0\le \tau\le 5$ and $h(4-\tau)=3$ on $2\le \tau\le 4$, with both signals zero elsewhere. Use the positive overlap area to find $y(4)$.
distractor_plan: Anticipate giving a negative value despite both signals being positive.
Anticipate using only one signal height as the area.
Anticipate using the full width of one signal instead of the overlap width.
Anticipate adding heights instead of multiplying them.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: At fixed output time $t=3$, a graph shows $x(\tau)=2$ on $0\le \tau\le 4$ and $h(3-\tau)=1$ on $1\le \tau\le 3$, with both signals zero elsewhere. Use the overlap area to find $y(3)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the product is positive on the overlap and conclude that $y(3)=4$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Keeps the same fixed-time area routine but makes the sign of the output an explicit part of the interpretation.
solution_step_plan: Identify that both signal values are positive on the overlap.
Read the overlap interval from the plot.
Multiply the positive heights to get the positive product height.
Compute the positive rectangle area.
State that the positive area adds to the output value.
practice_variation_axes: Vary the positive heights.
Vary the overlap width.
Keep both signals entirely above the axis.
Use one clean rectangular product region.

outline_section.handoff_notes: Make the sign reasoning explicit; this prepares the next section where the product falls below the axis.

prompt_blocks.text: At fixed output time $t=4$, the graph shows $x(\tau)=1$ on $0\le \tau\le 5$ and $h(4-\tau)=3$ on $2\le \tau\le 4$, with both signals zero elsewhere.
Use the positive overlap area to find $y(4)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Both signals are positive on the overlap, so the product area adds to the output. The overlap is $2\le \tau\le 4$, with width 2, and the product height is $1\cdot 3=3$. Therefore $y(4)=3\cdot 2=6$.

prompt_blocks.text: Two panels use the same input $x(\tau)=1$ on $0\le \tau\le 5$. In the first panel, $h(1-\tau)=4$ on $-1\le \tau\le 2$. In the second panel, $h(4-\tau)=1$ on $2\le \tau\le 5$. All signals are zero elsewhere.
Which comparison between $y(1)$ and $y(4)$ is correct?

choice_blocks.text: Both outputs are zero because the shifted responses differ.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: For $t=1$, the overlap is $0\le \tau\le 2$, so the width is 2 and the product height is $1\cdot 4=4$, giving area 8. For $t=4$, the overlap is $2\le \tau\le 5$, so the width is 3 and the product height is $1\cdot 1=1$, giving area 3. Since $8>3$, $y(1)>y(4)$.

question_policy.practice_question_model: A graph shows $x(\tau)$ supported on $0\le \tau\le 2$ and $h(5-\tau)$ supported on $3\le \tau\le 4$, with no overlap. What is $y(5)$?
distractor_plan: Anticipate computing the area of one signal instead of the product area.
Anticipate using the gap length as an output value.
Anticipate multiplying heights despite no shared interval.
Anticipate assuming every fixed output time must produce a nonzero value.

solution_step_plan: Read the support interval of $x(\tau)$.
Read the support interval of $h(5-\tau)$.
State that the intervals do not overlap.
Conclude that the product is zero for every $\tau$.
State the convolution output value as zero.

Vary the gap size.
Keep finite rectangular supports so no-overlap recognition is the central move.

prompt_blocks.text: At fixed output time $t=6$, a graph shows $x(\tau)$ supported on $1\le \tau\le 3$ and $h(6-\tau)$ supported on $4\le \tau\le 5$, with no overlap.
What is $y(6)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The two support intervals are separated: $[1,3]\cap[4,5]=\varnothing$. Since there is no $\tau$-value where both factors are nonzero, $x(\tau)h(6-\tau)=0$ for every $\tau$. The product area is therefore zero, so $y(6)=0$.

question_policy.practice_question_model: A graph shows $x(\tau)$ supported on $0\le \tau\le 2$ and $h(5-\tau)$ supported on $3\le \tau\le 4$, with no overlap. What is $y(5)$?
distractor_plan: Anticipate computing the area of one signal instead of the product area.
Anticipate using the gap length as an output value.
Anticipate multiplying heights despite no shared interval.
Anticipate assuming every fixed output time must produce a nonzero value.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: At fixed output time $t=5$, a graph shows $x(\tau)$ supported on $0\le \tau\le 2$ and $h(5-\tau)$ supported on $3\le \tau\le 4$. Use overlap area to determine $y(5)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Conclude that there is no overlap interval, so $x(\tau)h(5-\tau)=0$ everywhere and $y(5)=0$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Completes the overlap-area cases by showing that separated supports produce zero output rather than a positive or negative area.
solution_step_plan: Read the support interval of $x(\tau)$.
Read the support interval of $h(5-\tau)$.
State that the intervals do not overlap.
Conclude that the product is zero for every $\tau$.
State the convolution output value as zero.
practice_variation_axes: Vary which support interval lies to the left.
Vary the fixed output time label.
Vary the gap size.
Keep finite rectangular supports so no-overlap recognition is the central move.

outline_section.handoff_notes: Use this as the terminal contrast case: zero comes from no shared product interval, not from cancellation.

prompt_blocks.text: At fixed output time $t=2$, a graph shows $x(\tau)$ supported on $3\le \tau\le 6$ and $h(2-\tau)$ supported on $0\le \tau\le 2$, with no overlap.
What is $y(2)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The support intervals do not share any $\tau$-values: $[3,6]\cap[0,2]=\varnothing$. The output is not the area of one signal or the gap length; it is the signed area of the product. Because the product is zero everywhere, $y(2)=0$.

images.lesson_core_move: Interpret each convolution output value as the signed area of the product over the tau-interval where x(tau) overlaps the flipped-shifted impulse response h(t-tau).
images.section_title: Recognizing Zero Output from No Overlap Area
images.image_description: Aligned rectangular signal plots on a shared tau-axis for fixed output time t=5. Top plot: x(tau) is supported on 0<=tau<=2 and zero elsewhere. Middle plot: h(5-tau) is supported on 3<=tau<=4 and zero elsewhere. Leave a visible gap between tau=2 and tau=3 and label it no overlap. Do not shade any common interval. Bottom product-area panel: show x(tau)h(5-tau)=0 for all tau, with no product rectangle and a label area = 0 = y(5). Include tau-axis labels and endpoints 0, 2, 3, and 4.

outline_section.section_title: Recognizing Zero Output from No Overlap Area
outline_section.learning_goal: Recognize that if $x(\tau)$ and $h(t_0-\tau)$ have no overlapping nonzero $\tau$-interval, then the product area is zero and $y(t_0)=0$.
